title: APPLICATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS FOR FORMING THE SAFETY STOCK MATRIX IN RETAIL TRADE: PROMPT ENGINEERING METHODOLOGY
source: Financial Strategies of Innovative Economic Development
authors: Serhii Cheverda; Nataliia Maksyshko; S. M. Butenko; I. О. Dubyna
keywords: prompt engineering; large language models; retail inventory management; intermittent demand; small retail trade; Claude Sonnet 4.6
topics: Supply Chain and Inventory Management; Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society; Forecasting Techniques and Applications
abstract: The article investigates the practical foundations of applying large language models (LLM) of artificial intelligence for automated formation of a safety stock matrix in small retail trade. The object of the study is the «Kamilla» retail network (Tiachiv, Zakarpattia region) – five household chemicals and hygiene goods stores with a centralized warehouse infrastructure. It is established that approximately 80% of the network’s assortment positions are characterized by intermittent (irregular) demand, which makes effective application of classical time series forecasting methods impossible and necessitates adaptive analytical tools. It is shown that the transition from decentralized to centralized product placement increases the inventory utilization ratio from 53% to 71%, releasing over UAH 1 million of frozen working capital. A comparative testing of four free LLM platforms – Microsoft Copilot, OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Anthropic Claude – was conducted using a unified query. It is established that the Claude Sonnet 4.6 model in Extended Thinking mode demonstrates the highest analytical efficiency for structured business data. A three-stage methodology of iterative prompt engineering has been developed and tested: structuring instructions, delegating the choice of forecasting method to the model depending on the time series type, and implementing cross-verification mechanisms for result completeness. A cloud solution architecture based on the integration of Claude AI and Google Drive is proposed, which reduces the weekly order formation cycle to 3–5 minutes without direct financial implementation costs. The practical value of the study lies in providing small business managers with a systematic, reproducible, and zero-cost framework for inventory decision support.

title: Area- and Utilization-Efficient LLM Accelerator With Fused Speculative Decoding for Edge-Side Inference
source: IEEE Transactions on Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) Systems
authors: Kaiqi Chen; Zikang Zhou; Yaqi Chen; Jun Hyun Han
keywords: large language model inference; speculative decoding; edge inference; hardware accelerators; matrix multiplication; parameter sharing; off-chip memory access; inference latency; FPGA; area efficiency; energy efficiency; arithmetic intensity
topics: Embedded Systems Design Techniques; Advanced Neural Network Applications; Low-power high-performance VLSI design
abstract: The inference of large language models (LLMs) on edge devices has always been a challenge, the autoregressive inference and enormous number of parameters result in long inference latency. Although speculative decoding is proposed for inference acceleration, it poses challenges for hardware accelerator design, as the differing computational characteristics of the drafting and verification stages make it difficult to optimize both chip area and hardware utilization. This brief introduces fused speculative decoding (FSD) to optimize LLM inference on edge devices by unifying all the operations to general matrix multiplications during inference. The proposed FSD-Infer algorithm fuses the drafting and verification phases of conventional speculative decoding and enables weight sharing, reducing off-chip memory access, and inference latency without requiring retraining or fine-tuning. For hardware, we introduce FSD-Acc, an area- and utilization-efficient hardware accelerator that efficiently executes the fused operations enabled by FSD-Infer. Experimental results show that compared with autoregressive inference, FSD-Infer reduces EMA by up to 26.11%, enhances arithmetic intensity by$10.26\times $, and speeds up GPU inference by up to$1.38\times $. When deployed on Xilinx ZCU102 FPGA board at 200 MHz working frequency, FSD-Acc achieves the best area efficiency and energy efficiency, outperforming the state-of-the-art LLM accelerator for edge inference by$2.53\times $(TPS/kDSP),$5.90\times $(TPS/kLUT) and$2.02\times $, respectively.

title: Artificial intelligence algorithms for complex industrial optimization
authors: Wenqiang Zhang; Mitsuo Gen
keywords: industrial optimization; large language models; LLM agents; constraint acquisition; human-AI collaboration; closed-loop adaptation; multi-objective optimization; supply chain optimization; uncertainty quantification; explainable AI; human-in-the-loop
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society; Scheduling and Optimization Algorithms; Process Optimization and Integration
abstract: We organize the research needs around three connected challenges: AI-assisted problem formulation and structural representation; scalable optimization of coupled resources and supply chains; and closed-loop adaptation in dynamic, uncertain, and multi-objective environments. Two requirements cut across all three challenges: structure-aware integration of optimization, learning, and simulation; and operational validation, human-AI collaboration, and accountability. In the latter, information, tasks, and decision authority are allocated among domain experts, operators, AI assistants and agents, optimizers, and simulators according to risk and context (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Industrial optimization begins before a solver is selected. Relevant information is distributed across data systems, engineering documents, regulations, and expert practice. These sources differ in timing, vocabulary, and reliability. Model formulation requires identification of the decisions, objectives, constraints, uncertainties, and couplings that define the operational problem. Translating an agreed description into equations is only one part of that task.Methods for constraint acquisition can infer candidate rules from examples and expert queries (Bessiere et al., 2017), while decision-focused approaches can optimize predictive models for downstream decision quality (Donti et al., 2017;Wilder et al., 2019). Rules inferred from data or text remain provisional until they are checked against actual operations. Each candidate rule requires verification of its provenance, scope, conflicts with other rules, and operational consequences before it enters a decision model. Human skills, decision rights, and handoff responsibilities may themselves be part of the modeled structure, particularly when tasks can move between people and automated components (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents can mediate between informal descriptions and formal optimization models. They can propose formulations, generate solver code, and assign modeling or verification tasks to specialized components (Zhang et al., 2024a;Xiao et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2026). Recent work that combines LLM-based extraction with reusable modeling graphs and expert-defined templates illustrates a more controlled division of responsibility (Li et al., 2026). These outputs remain candidate models. Solver execution can expose coding errors or infeasibility, but it cannot establish semantic completeness or show that an omitted business rule is inconsequential.A traceable modeling loop records how constraints are acquired and classified, who validates them, how uncertainty and problem structure are represented, and when operational change triggers model revision. If the resulting problem is infeasible, the algorithm needs to identify the conflicting assumptions and return either an interpretable relaxation or a safe recovery action. Evaluation then turns on downstream decision performance under missing or changing information; fluent model generation alone is insufficient.The computational burden of large industrial optimization problems arises from both problem size and coordination across resources, organizations, and time scales. Machines, workforce capabilities, energy supply, inventory, and transport capacity are coupled through shared constraints, but their influence on system performance is unequal and state dependent. A disruption can shift the bottleneck from equipment to technicians, spare parts, storage, or transport. Algorithms need representations and sensitivity measures that identify the binding couplings and detect when those relationships change.In distributed scheduling, job-to-factory assignment and within-factory sequencing are interdependent (Naderi and Ruiz, 2010). Across a supply chain, procurement, production, inventory, and delivery decisions are made over different planning horizons. Solving these stages separately can shift costs, delays, or emissions downstream; even under restricted assumptions, integrated production-inventory-delivery models are computationally demanding (Gen et al., 2008;Li et al., 2017). Coordination also involves organizations, human planners, and AI agents that hold different information and decision rights. Recent supply-chain research on agentic AI accordingly treats human-agent roles and organizational constraints as design choices rather than assuming full autonomy (Trifone et al., 2026).Decomposition and mathematical programming can exploit sparsity and explicit constraint structure, while evolutionary algorithms and large-neighborhood search can explore difficult discrete and nonconvex search spaces (Yu and Gen, 2010;Pisinger and Ropke, 2010). A central design question is how to balance global exploration with local improvement. Global moves reallocate orders, capacity, and supply-chain flows; local moves refine sequences, routes, and maintenance schedules. Learned components may select neighborhoods, warm starts, decompositions, or algorithm configurations. Their value depends on preserving global consistency while reducing end-to-end decision time and resource use. A learned policy may improve one subproblem yet render another infeasible when cross-stage constraints are omitted, represented too coarsely, or invalidated by a disruption. Learned guidance also needs to recognize when a fixed decomposition is no longer valid.Multiple objectives introduce an additional tension between computational efficiency and decision effectiveness. Efficiency concerns whether an algorithm returns an answer before the decision deadline. Effectiveness covers feasibility, solution-set quality and diversity, and alignment with decision-maker preferences (Deb et al., 2002;Zhang et al., 2024b). Automated program search can generate heuristics and search rules, including variants for multi-objective optimization (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024;Yao et al., 2025). Their performance remains uncertain when the evaluation function overlooks cross-stage couplings. Evaluation should establish whether local gains persist once supply-chain interactions are accounted for and whether a globally consistent plan can be produced on time.Demand, resource availability, prices, and customer priorities change over different time scales. Parameter uncertainty, observed disruptions, distribution shift, and structural change each call for a different response. Repeatedly running a static optimizer after every event does not by itself create a closed-loop strategy.A closed-loop algorithm links state estimation and prediction to model revision, optimization, execution, and feedback. Robust planning and reactive rescheduling play complementary roles and can be coordinated through rolling-horizon optimization, online learning, dynamic optimization, and calibrated simulation. Full regeneration may improve the objective value but increase schedule nervousness; local repair preserves stability but can lock in a poor global allocation (Vieira et al., 2003;Blackburn et al., 1986). Reinforcement learning can represent delayed consequences, but exploration in industrial systems must respect constraints during training and deployment. A high expected return does not establish acceptable tail risk or recoverability (García and Fernández, 2015;Wachi et al., 2024). Recent dynamic-scheduling work shows how a formal supervisor can restrict reinforcement learning to a safe, non-blocking operating space and support rapid recovery after disruptions (Wang et al., 2026).Digital twins are useful for stress testing only if their models remain valid under the disruptions that drive decisions (Tao et al., 2019). Emerging architectures connect digital twins, multiple agents, online multi-objective optimization, and human-robot collaboration (Huang et al., 2026). These combinations strengthen the case for a closed loop, but they also increase the number of interfaces whose state, latency, and failure modes need monitoring.Priorities assigned to cost, service, sustainability, resilience, and workload may also change during a disruption. Adaptation therefore requires more than repeated static Pareto optimization. The algorithm needs to choose among continuing or repairing the current plan, re-optimizing, updating the model, and escalating the decision to a human decision-maker. Task and decision authority may also need to shift as risk, AI confidence, human workload, and time pressure change. Evaluation needs to report feasibility under distributional and structural shifts, tail-risk and recovery metrics, and operational gains net of excessive plan changes.Hybrid algorithmic architectures are justified only when their components perform distinct, necessary functions, their interfaces can be validated, and the integrated method outperforms a strong but simpler baseline (Fan et al., 2026;Wiberg et al., 2026). Learning can estimate uncertain states or surrogate models and select search controls when equivalent information is unavailable within the operational deadline. Mathematical and constraint programming can enforce explicit feasibility logic and provide bounds. Evolutionary algorithms are useful for discrete, nonconvex, black-box, or preference-sensitive search, whereas simulation represents behavior that is difficult to express analytically.The interfaces between components deserve equal scrutiny because they govern information exchange, uncertainty propagation, and failure detection. A learned initialization may accelerate a solver yet fail under distribution shift. Likewise, a high-fidelity simulation may consume the computation needed for adequate stress testing. Ablation studies need to test both individual contributions and failures at component interfaces under the same operational budget.A learning-based or generative component may propose a formulation or heuristic; a solver, simulator, or explicit checker can then test it. The inclusion of every added component should be justified by a verifiable improvement in decision quality. This division of responsibility is especially important for LLM-based agents, whose ability to orchestrate tools does not remove the need for formal checks and controlled access to operational systems.Operational reliability depends on how an algorithm interacts with enterprise data flows, shop-floor execution systems, and human decision-makers. Stale state information, interface mismatches, human overrides, and execution deviations can all change the optimization problem. Monitoring, rollback, reoptimization, escalation, and revalidation are consequently part of the algorithm lifecycle.The appropriate unit of analysis is the hybrid decision team rather than the AI component in isolation.Its performance depends on how information, tasks, and authority are distributed among operators, managers, AI agents, optimization solvers, and organizational units. Human participants can contribute tacit knowledge and handle exceptions, but poor handoffs or unclear authority can delay responses and obscure accountability. Experimental evidence from AI-assisted production indicates that team organization affects failure recovery through the frequency and quality of communication (Krzywdzinski et al., 2026). Semantic models for dynamic work sharing offer one way to represent changing human and artificial roles, although their contribution must ultimately be tested through team and system outcomes (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Accordingly, evaluation should include communication quality, handoff latency, calibrated reliance, intervention workload, recovery performance, and operational outcomes alongside conventional algorithmic metrics. Explanations need separate scrutiny: in a job-shop scheduling experiment, brief AI rationales increased behavioral reliance without necessarily improving understanding (Saßmannshausen et al., 2026). Trust, reliance, and decision correctness are distinct measures.Claims of improvement require comparison against competitive optimization, learning, and engineering baselines under matched end-to-end resource budgets. Those budgets include data preparation, model development, computation, simulation, and human effort. Experiments need to vary coupling strength, constraint tightness, disruption severity, distribution shift, and decision deadlines rather than instance size alone. Studies should also report prediction quality, optimization quality, and operational value separately. Optimization quality includes feasibility, optimality gap, regret, and Pareto-front approximation quality; operational value includes plan stability, service performance, recovery time, and integration effort.Fluent formulations and executable code do not establish correctness. Grounded in solver functions, LLM interfaces can nevertheless support infeasibility diagnosis, sensitivity analysis, and what-if or why-not queries (Chen et al., 2025). High-consequence decisions still require traceable constraints, validated alternatives, controlled system access, and explicit human authority over rollback and escalation.The three challenges span problem formulation and structural representation, scalable optimization of coupled resources and supply chains, and closed-loop adaptation. Success depends on a faithful operational model, coordination of coupled decisions within the available time, and revision of those decisions without sacrificing feasibility or stability. Structure-aware integration determines whether the algorithmic components work together; operational validation, human-AI collaboration, and accountability determine whether gains at one stage translate into system-level performance.Prediction accuracy, average reward, isolated benchmark gains, and the addition of another AI component provide incomplete evidence of progress. The stronger standard is better decision quality under realistic constraints, coupling, and change, together with communication and authority arrangements that support timely intervention and recovery. Ultimately, an industrial AI algorithm needs to solve the right problem within the decision deadline and continue to produce feasible, stable, and controllable decisions as operating conditions change.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Civil Justice: U.S. Practice, Policy, and Principles
source: The American Journal of Comparative Law
authors: S I Strong
keywords: United States; AI regulation; automated decision-making; transparency and accountability; generative AI; retrieval-augmented generation; rule-based AI; access to justice; judicial capacity building; public trust in AI; AI policy; comparative law; AI governance; artificial intelligence in courts; artificial intelligence in criminal justice
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Law; Digitalization, Law, and Regulation; Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
abstract: In the coming years, artificial intelligence (AI) will change the legal profession and the civil justice system significantly and irrevocably. While AI may often be useful and even beneficial, certain guardrails must be established to ensure the quality of justice is not diminished. When determining the appropriate boundaries of national law and practice, it can be helpful to consider how other jurisdictions approach the issue at hand. The International Academy of Comparative Law (IACL) has undertaken precisely such a study regarding AI, with findings to be published in an edited volume.1 The current analysis constitutes an excerpt from the national report for the United States. This Report follows the basic structure established by the general rapporteurs for the IACL comparative study, although the responses have been edited for space. The discussion begins in Section I with a general overview of AI in the United States, including both definitions and strategic initiatives. Next, Section II covers the legal and regulatory framework for AI in U.S. civil justice systems, addressing governance concerns both generally and specifically with respect to the judiciary. Section III focuses on key issues in civil justice, including an overview of existing case law; a discussion of AI’s role, benefits, and risks; the extent to which the United States allows fully automated decision-making; and transparency and accountability of AI systems. In Section IV, the Report addresses current or planned models of AI in civil justice and examines AI systems involving various types of court activity. This section also discusses capacity-building for judges and lawyers in the area of AI as well as public perception and trust of AI in civil justice systems. After reviewing economic and access to justice concerns in Section V, the Report provides an overview of future development and challenges in Section VI. Definitions are important in the world of AI. Processes vary widely and include such diverse technologies as rule-based AI, generative AI, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).2 Each of these mechanisms gives rise to different practical and policy concerns, though most laws, policies, and guidelines do not distinguish among the different systems. While there is no single definition of AI that is used consistently throughout the United States,3 one influential definition indicates that AI is a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. Artificial intelligence systems use machine and human-based inputs to- (A) perceive real and virtual environments; (B) abstract such perceptions into models through analysis in an automated manner; and (C) use model inference to formulate options for information or action.4 State-level definitions vary significantly,5 although it is unclear whether and to what extent those variations will survive in the wake of Executive Order 14,365, which seeks to limit “excessive State regulation” of AI.6 At the time of writing, it appeared that the Executive Order was likely to be challenged on constitutional grounds, though no such action had yet been brought.7 The federal judiciary has engaged with AI at both the national and local levels. The most critical work at the national level is being done by the Judicial Conference.8 The Judicial Conference appears to have first considered AI in early 2024, when the Committee on Court Administration and Court Assistance reported on the emerging use of AI in preparing judicial submissions and increasing efficiency in court administration and the Committee on Federal-State Jurisdiction discussed a report from chief justices of various state courts concerning the effect of AI on the courts and the practice of law.9 The next year, the Judicial Conference issued a five-year strategic report that reflected an intent to “[e]stablish an AI governance framework to guide responsible adoption of AI and to manage risks and challenges presented by these new and evolving technologies.”10 The Judicial Conference’s Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules (Evidence Committee) has been particularly active with respect to AI.11 For example, the Evidence Committee has considered whether to adopt a new Rule 707 on machine learning and a new Rule 901 on digital replicas, also known as deepfakes.12 While the new rule on deepfakes remained in committee at the time of writing, a public consultation regarding Rule 707 was released in August 2025, with the public comment period concluding in February 2026.13 Other parts of the federal government, most notably the U.S. Copyright Office, have also taken steps to address deepfakes.14 The federal judiciary has also addressed AI through rules and orders promulgated by individual federal courts and judges.15 Several courts have cautioned litigants about the use of AI and noted the need to confirm and verify the accuracy of all pleadings and submissions.16 Individual judges have also adopted standing orders relating to the use of AI by litigants, although no known order describes whether and to what extent the judge can or will use AI.17 Instead, orders typically require litigants and/or counsel to ensure submissions are accurate by personally reviewing any AI-generated content.18 Some orders include explanations about why AI in judicial settings is problematic, perhaps for the benefit of pro se litigants who might not otherwise be aware of the challenges of AI in legal settings.19 The executive branch has addressed AI through a series of executive orders beginning in 2019.20 Several orders note that the use of AI must not only comply with the Constitution but must also maintain values that are central to civil justice, including public trust and the protection of privacy, civil rights title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Supply Chain Optimization Models Challenges and Future Directions
source: International Journal of Scientific Research in Computer Science Engineering and Information Technology
authors: Mr. Deepak Mehta
keywords: artificial intelligence; supply chain optimization; demand forecasting; inventory optimization; supplier selection; production scheduling; supply chain network design; reinforcement learning; multi-agent reinforcement learning; generative AI; large language models; supply chain resilience; explainability; data quality; privacy-preserving AI; digital twin
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society; Supply Chain and Inventory Management; Big Data and Business Intelligence
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a key driver of change in the supply chain, particularly in its ability to predict, adapt and optimise in complex, uncertain environments. The review covers AI-based supply chain optimization models, applications, performance, challenges and future research directions. The study covers the key AI techniques, such as Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Reinforcement Learning (RL), Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), and hybrid AI–metaheuristic methods. Such methods are used for demand forecasting, inventory optimization, supplier selection, procurement, production scheduling, transportation, routing and supply chain network design. The review notes benefits of AI-based optimization, such as better forecasting accuracy, cost efficiency, resource utilization, adaptability, operational responsiveness, and supply chain resilience. Despite these advances, there are major hurdles such as data quality, interoperability, limited model explainability, cybersecurity and privacy issues, computational demands, scalability, and lack of empirical validation. The results highlight the importance of the development of integrated, reliable, explainable, and adaptive AI optimization frameworks that are able to assist with real-time decision-making. There is a need for further research on Generative AI, multi-agent systems, digital twins, sustainable optimization, privacy-preserving AI, and large-scale empirical validation, to further enhance practical supply chain implementation.

title: ASSESING THE STRUCTURED DATA INFERENCE CAPABILITY OF LOCAL LANGUAGE MODELS ON EDGE DEVICES FOR IOT SYSTEM COORDINATION
source: SCIENTIFIC JOURNAL OF TAN TRAO UNIVERSITY
authors: PHAN VAN NAM; DO HUU SON
keywords: local language models; edge computing; Internet of Things; hallucination mitigation; home automation; latency
topics: IoT and Edge/Fog Computing; Internet of Things and AI; Topic Modeling
abstract: The current dependence of IoT systems on cloud computing is causing many limitations regarding latency, security risks, and stability. To overcome this, the study proposes shifting processing capabilities to edge devices using Local Language Models (Local LLMs). To resolve the conflict between the free text of LLMs and central control systems, we apply an output format coercion technique, forcing the model to interpolate intent and output data strictly adhering to the JSON command structure. Experiments on simulated high-performance edge device hardware show that this method completely eliminates format hallucination, achieving a 100% successful JSON parsing rate. Regarding performance, the token generation speed (TPS) ranges from 37 to over 184 tokens/second, the time to first token (TTFT) is under 5 ms, the end-to-end latency takes only 0,16 to 1,2 seconds, and the peak VRAM consumption is under 4,5 GB. These results excellently meet the real-time standards of smart home experiences, affirming the feasibility of the local AIoT coordination solution.

title: Assessing the use of automatic speech recognition and large language models for individuals with language impairments
authors: Gelei Xu; Haoxinran Yu; Lixuan Wei; Yuxuan Liu; Yuxuan Liu; Chenhui Xu; Jiajie Li; Ahmed Abbasi; Jinjun Xiong; Xiufan Yu; Zhi Zheng; Yiyu Shi; Ruiyang Qin
keywords: language impairment; speech recognition; large language models; edge computing; disfluency; fillers; evaluation framework; interpretability; robustness; inclusive healthcare; children and elderly
topics: Speech Recognition and Synthesis; Speech and dialogue systems; Voice and Speech Disorders
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) have attracted much attention for healthcare applications, demonstrating strong potential in automating conversational interactions. However, cloud-hosted LLMs pose major data privacy concerns when processing Protected Health Information. Moreover, current LLM-based systems rely on text input/output, creating substantial barriers for users, such as children and older adults, who may have difficulty typing. To mitigate these challenges, there has been growing interest in developing edge device-based, voice-enabled LLM systems. Running LLMs on edge devices minimizes the risks of PHI leaking to the cloud, while automatic speech recognition (ASR) eliminates the need for text-based inputs. Despite these advantages, existing ASRs convert speech into word-by-word text, which often contains disfluencies and fillers (e.g., ”um”, ”hum”) and grammatical errors, especially for individuals with language impairments. This noisy input can significantly degrade the performance of LLMs, yet this chained issue remains under-explored in healthcare applications. To address this critical gap, we conducted a systematic analysis through comparison studies and ablation experiments to identify key factors affecting the performance of edge-based ASR-LLM systems when used by individuals with language impairments. Furthermore, we proposed an evaluation framework for speech-enabled AI healthcare to emphasize both interpretability and robustness, paving the way for more inclusive and secure conversational healthcare solutions.

title: Attention Distribution-Aware Softmax for NPU-Accelerated On-Device Inference of LLMs: An Edge-Oriented Approximation Design
authors: Sanoop Sadheerthan; Min-Jie Hsu; Chih-Hsiang Huang; Yin-Tien Wang
keywords: softmax approximation; exponential function approximation; attention allocation; neural processing units; edge computing; particle swarm optimization; piecewise polynomial approximation; look-up table; fixed-point arithmetic; transformer models; TinyLlama
topics: Numerical Methods and Algorithms; Advanced Neural Network Applications; Low-power high-performance VLSI design
abstract: Low-power NPUs enable on-device LLM inference through efficient integer and fixed-point algebra, yet their lack of native exponential support makes Transformer softmax a critical performance bottleneck. Existing NPU kernels approximate ex using uniform piecewise polynomials to enable O(1) SIMD indexing, but this wastes computation by applying high-degree arithmetic indiscriminately in every segment. Conversely, fully adaptive approaches maximize statistical fidelity but introduce pipeline stalls due to comparator-based boundary search. To bridge this gap, we propose an attention distribution-aware softmax that uses Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to define non-uniform segments and variable polynomial degrees, prioritizing finer granularity and lower arithmetic complexity in attention-dense regions. To ensure efficiency, we snap boundaries into a 128-bin LUT, enabling O(1) retrieval of segment parameters without branching. Inference measurements show that this favors low-degree execution, minimizing exp-kernel overhead. Using TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat as a testbed, the proposed weighted design reduces cycles per call exp kernel (CPC) by 18.5% versus an equidistant uniform Degree-4 baseline and 13.1% versus uniform Degree-3, while preserving ranking fidelity. These results show that grid-snapped, variable-degree approximation can improve softmax efficiency while largely preserving attention ranking fidelity, enabling accurate edge LLM inference.

title: Automated Detection of Deceptive Design Patterns on University Websites: A Comparative Analysis of Browser-Based Tools and LLM-Based Approaches
authors: Karol Król
keywords: university websites; institutional websites; automated detection; browser extension; large language models; GPT; heuristic evaluation; web accessibility; Polish universities
topics: Usability and User Interface Design; Web Data Mining and Analysis; Innovative Human-Technology Interaction
abstract: Although recent years have seen an emergence of tools for automated identification of deceptive design patterns on websites, their scope and reliability remain understudied. Institutional websites are a particularly interesting research domain. They have an extensive information structure and shape the conditions of user interaction. The purpose of the article is to empirically evaluate signs of deceptive design patterns on Polish universities’ websites and analyse how they are identified using automated analytical tools. The study covers all public universities in Poland (N = 65). The analysis involved automated tools representing different methodological underpinnings, including web browser extensions and GPT language model-based analytical procedures. The study pinpoints significant differences in the paradigms behind the results provided by the two methods. Browser extensions yielded only qualitative suggestions of potential problems. They did not generate complete and comparable quantitative results for the entire population of the investigated websites. Results from the heuristic Real-Time Deceptive Pattern Auditor (RTDPA) were highly concentrated (mean 90.03, median 90, SD = 1.55, and interval 80–95), which may suggest limited discriminatory power for this website collection. In contrast, the rule-based Structural Interface Risk Screening (SIRS) revealed a much greater differentiation of results (mean 89.23, median 90, SD = 11.50, and interval 50–100). The association between the results from the two procedures was very weak (r = 0.089, p ≈ 0.48), which indicates their limited quantitative comparability. These findings indicate that the current capabilities of automated tools offer merely fragmented detection of selected deceptive design patterns, instead of a complete systemic diagnosis of the problem. Although they are measurement tools by declaration, the solutions can offer only preliminary screening, flagging potential risk areas. Not differentiating between risk signalling and actual measurement may lead to the illusion of automated precision.

title: AUTOMATED SKILLS ORCHESTRATION: TEACHING AGENTIC AI ARCHITECTURE THROUGH DETERMINISTIC EXECUTION FRAMEWORKS
keywords: agentic AI; deterministic execution; AI agent architecture
topics: AI-based Problem Solving and Planning; Artificial Intelligence Applications; Teaching and Learning Programming
abstract: Agentic AI systems-autonomous workflows capable of multi-step reasoning, tool invocation, and selfcorrection-are reshaping how information systems professionals work.Yet a tension underlies them all: large language models are stochastic by design, producing variable outputs through temperaturecontrolled token sampling, while business processes demand consistency and reproducibility.This paper proposes a three-layer skills architecture for teaching IS students to navigate that tension: a Directive layer (Markdown standard operating procedures that define intent), an Orchestration layer (LLM-powered decision-making on platforms such as AWS Bedrock), and an Execution layer (deterministic Python that handles computation, API calls, and data processing).Drawing on the practitioner-developed skill pattern, we formalize the architecture as a pedagogical framework, apply it across IS domains-database management, accounting, business intelligence, and project management-and illustrate it with a skill deployed in production.The central argument is that IS programs face a consequential choice: teach students to use AI tools, a competency with a short half-life as tools change and tool use is itself automated, or teach them to architect AI systems, a competency that remains valuable regardless of which tools prevail because the architectural principles are invariant.Students who build skills through this framework are not learning to use AI tools; they are learning to design the systems that use them.

title: Automating Computation Independent Model Elicitation in MDA using Task-Oriented Dialogue with In-Context Learning
source: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications
authors: Mohamed El Ayadi; Yassine Rhazali; Mohammed Lahmer
keywords: computation independent model; model-driven architecture; requirements analysis; task-oriented dialogue; in-context learning; large language models; chatbots; domain-specific languages; BPMN; UML use cases; natural language understanding; model validation
topics: Model-Driven Software Engineering Techniques; Speech and dialogue systems; Software Engineering Techniques and Practices
abstract: The Computation Independent Model (CIM) is a cornerstone of the Object Management Group's (OMG) Model-Driven Architecture (MDA), capturing business requirements and domain knowledge independent of specific technologies. However, the elicitation of CIM requirements is often a manual, time-consuming, and error-prone process, susceptible to ambiguities inherent in natural language. Traditional Natural Language Understanding (NLU) approaches, particularly intent-based systems, exhibit limitations in scalability, contextual understanding, and handling the nuanced, evolving nature of complex requirements. This study proposes a novel approach that integrates Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) systems with the In-Context Learning (ICL) capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate and enhance CIM requirements elicitation. The proposed framework features a conversational agent that guides stakeholders through structured dialogue flows, translating their natural language inputs into a formal CIM-Domain Specific Language (CIM-DSL). These DSL commands are then transformed into CIM artifacts, such as Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams and Unified Modeling Language (UML) use cases. The approach emphasizes quality assurance through interactive validation, consistency checks, and strategies to mitigate LLM limitations. We anticipate this method will significantly improve the accuracy, completeness, and efficiency of CIM construction, thereby strengthening the foundation of the MDA lifecycle.

title: Automating Cyber Risk Assessment With Public LLMs: An Expert-Validated Framework and Comparative Analysis
authors: Nezih Mahmut Unal; Barış Çeliktaş
keywords: cybersecurity risk assessment; large language models; LLM agents; GPT-4o; Gemini; CVSS; NIST SP 800-30
topics: Information and Cyber Security; Web Application Security Vulnerabilities; Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning
abstract: Traditional cyber risk assessment methodologies face a critical dilemma: they are either quantitative yet static and context-agnostic (e.g., CVSS), or context-aware yet highly labor-intensive and subjective (e.g., NIST SP 800-30). Consequently, organizations struggle to scale risk assessment to match the pace of evolving threats. This paper presents an automated, context-aware risk assessment framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of publicly available Large Language Models (LLMs) to operationalize expert knowledge. Rather than positioning the LLM as the final decision-maker, the framework decouples semantic interpretation from risk scoring authority through a transparent, deterministic Dynamic Metric Engine. Unlike complex black-box machine learning models, our approach anchors the AI’s reasoning to this expert-validated metric schema, with weights derived using the Rank Order Centroid (ROC) method from a survey of 101 cybersecurity professionals. We evaluated the framework through a comparative study involving 15 diverse real-world vulnerability scenarios (C1−C15) and three supplementary sensitivity stress tests (C16−C18). The validation scenarios were independently assessed by a cohort of ten senior human experts and two state-of-the-art LLM agents (GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash). The results show that the LLM-driven agents achieve scoring consistency closely aligned with the human median (Pearsonrranging from 0.9390 to 0.9717, Spearman ρ from 0.8472 to 0.9276) against a highly reliable expert baseline (Cronbach’s α = 0.996), while reducing the assessment cycle time by more than 100× (averaging under 4 seconds per case vs. a human average of 6 minutes). Furthermore, a dedicated context sensitivity analysis (C13−C15) indicates that the framework adapts risk scores based on organizational context (e.g., SME vs. Critical Infrastructure) for identical technical vulnerabilities. Importantly, the system is designed not merely to replicate expert intuition, but to enforce bounded, policy-consistent risk evaluation under predefined governance constraints. Overall, these findings suggest that commercially available LLMs, when constrained by expert-validated metric schemas, can support reproducible, transparent, and real-time risk assessments.

title: Autonomous Enterprise IVR Orchestration Using Agentic Artificial Intelligence: A Multi-Agent Framework for LLM-Based Reasoning, OpenAPI Tool Invocation, and Business Process Automation
source: International Journal of Intelligent Systems and Applications in Engineering
authors: Venkata Krishna Reddy Kovvuri
keywords: multi-agent systems; agentic AI; LLM reasoning; business process automation
topics: Speech and dialogue systems; AI in Service Interactions; Artificial Intelligence Applications
abstract: Enterprise IVR systems must have independent intelligence to go beyond predetermined workflows and human reliance. The proposed research is based on a multi-agent AI model that incorporates the notions of LLM reasoning, communication with OpenAPI tools, and automation of business processes. Performance of workflows on a synthetic IVR dataset and machine learning models is assessed, with a high accuracy of 93.80% of tasks, 95.30% API accuracy, and lower human escalation. The framework provides a demonstration of scalable autonomous orchestration and tackles issues of reliability and security within enterprise communication settings.

title: Benchmarking Reference-Free LLM Agent Robustness Under Schema, Policy, and Toolset Drift
authors: Moh. Hasbi Assidiqi; Daniyal Alghazzawi; Suaad Alarifi; Li Cheng
keywords: LLM agents; tool use; schema drift; policy drift; branch selection; GPT-4o-mini; Qwen3-32B; DeepSeek-V3
topics: AI-based Problem Solving and Planning; Topic Modeling; Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning
abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents fail when external interfaces evolve, yet most evaluations emphasize static competence rather than adaptation under drift. We studied this problem with controlled schema, policy, and toolset perturbations derived from tau2-bench retail tasks and distinguished between a reference-guided replay benchmark and reference-free adaptation. In a reference-guided exact-trajectory setting, GPT-4o mini reached 0.708 task success over 216 trials, establishing that the benchmark contains recoverable structure. We then evaluated five OpenRouter-served models—GPT-4o mini, GPT-4o, Kimi K2, DeepSeek V3, and Qwen3-32B—under a reference-free protocol scoring end-state task completion across 270 trials per model-condition cell (30 scenarios × 3 episodes × 3 drift families). Static baselines range from 0.130 to 0.432 across models. Blind replay consistently degrades reference-free task success relative to static for four of five models; Kimi K2 is the exception, for which both blind replay and rules-only significantly improve over the static baseline. Rules-only shows model-dependent effects, significantly improving for Kimi K2 and Qwen3-32B while showing no significant difference for the remaining three models. A normalization-ablation condition confirms that the drift-inversion layer is load-bearing for toolset drift; schema-obedience determines whether this layer is effective.Within the three evaluated drift types and controller conditions, the reference-guided replay advantage does not transfer to reference-free task success, and the primary barriers are hidden-state reconstruction and branch selection across multiple candidate orders and products.

title: ChatXmile : An LLM ‐Assisted Closed‐Loop Workflow for the System Dynamics Process
authors: Bo Hu; Bo Zhang; Justin Hoffmann; Michael Woywadt
keywords: large language models; system dynamics modeling; closed-loop workflow; model verification; model diagnostics; sensitivity analysis; scenario-based experiment; web-based modeling tool; model reliability
topics: Complex Systems and Decision Making; Modeling and Simulation Systems; Simulation Techniques and Applications
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper presents ChatXmile, a browser‐based method and web application (the ChatXmile system) that integrates large language models (LLMs) with deterministic, rule‐based software to streamline system dynamics modeling. In a closed‐loop workflow, an LLM generates or revises an XMILE model, which is then subjected to automated conformance and technical checks (schema and rule checks, units consistency, structural inspection, and executable trial runs). Diagnostics are fed back to guide targeted revisions. Once a model passes these checks, ChatXmile also supports generating structured narratives and HTML/JavaScript simulators to enable sensitivity analysis, extreme‐condition tests, time‐step adequacy checks, and scenario experiments. Overall, the approach establishes an auditable narrative–model–verification loop that supports reconstruction across sessions and improves the reliability and dissemination of system dynamics models.

title: Classical-First Selective Cascades for Resource-Constrained Phishing Email Detection
authors: Abdulaziz Saleh Alajaji
keywords: phishing email detection; linear support vector machine; TF-IDF features; DistilBERT; model drift monitoring; Internet of Things security; wireless sensor networks
topics: Spam and Phishing Detection; Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning; Text and Document Classification Technologies
abstract: Phishing email detection is a practical requirement for human-operated security and administration workflows, including mail gateways, security operations centre (SOC) triage queues, cloud dashboards, firmware-management portals, and other operational interfaces. In Internet-of-Things (IoT) and wireless sensor network (WSN) operations, compromise of such human-operated interfaces can open an initial-access path into the sensor-network management plane; however, the present study evaluates email body classifiers on public phishing email corpora rather than on-device IoT/WSN hardware. Email filtering must often run on low-cost servers, where running and storing a transformer for every message is costly in compute and memory, and opaque scores are hard to audit. We compare four model families on four public phishing email corpora: hand-engineered classifiers, high-vocabulary classical models, frozen-transformer classifiers, and a CPU-feasible fine-tuned DistilBERT reference. The strongest low-cost model is a Platt-calibrated Linear SVM with high-vocabulary TF-IDF features. It reaches F1 = 0.961 on the primary corpus, slightly exceeds the frozen DistilBERT baseline and is statistically indistinguishable from the fine-tuned DistilBERT reference in-domain, and requires 0.23 MB on disk with about 8 ms per email. This shows that transformer inference is not required for competitive accuracy on the evaluated in-domain corpora. We then evaluate the Calibrated Selective Cascade (CSC) as an operational routing layer: a calibrated low-cost arm handles most messages, while a validation-selected uncertainty band is deferred to a transformer arm. With the strong SVM arm, CSC yields only marginal in-domain F1 gains, but provides a tunable latency/deferral trade-off parameter and a monitorable drift signal. On an exploratory synthetic stress set of stylistically neutral, LLM-style phishing, no evaluated body-only model exceeds F1 around 0.46; closing this gap would require header-, URL-, identity-, and attachment-level signals.

title: Cloud-edge collaborative interpretable fault classification for helical tomotherapy systems via LLM–VLM reasoning
source: Journal of Cloud Computing Advances Systems and Applications
authors: Haonan Yang; Jie Guo; Yan Wang; Xingkun Zhang
keywords: helical tomotherapy; cloud-edge collaboration; large language models; vision-language models; medical image classification; industrial inspection; surface damage detection; structural anomaly detection; real-time fault diagnosis
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection; Multimodal Machine Learning Applications; Quality and Safety in Healthcare
abstract: Abstract Helical tomotherapy systems (HTS) involve complex multi-system integration, where equipment faults vary significantly in severity and demand high interpretability in automated diagnosis. With the increasing deployment of HTS across distributed clinical environments, there is a growing need for cloud-enabled intelligent fault detection systems that support scalable monitoring and centralized analysis. This study aims to develop an interpretable visual classification framework for HTS fault detection via cloud-edge collaboration between Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Based on adverse event records from 2023 to 2025 in our institution, we constructed a multi-category image dataset covering common HTS fault patterns, including Surface Damage, Deformation, Material Loss, Contamination, Texture Anomaly, Intensity Abnormality, and Structural Breakage. We propose a medical-oriented Retrieval-driven Reasoning framework (RdR-Med) for fault classification. Specifically, LLMs are deployed on the cloud to extract category-relevant fault descriptors and structural abnormality patterns, forming a structured retrieval database. During inference, edge devices perform lightweight visual feature extraction, while the cloud executes retrieval and multi-step deliberative reasoning via VLMs, enabling explicit reasoning before producing the final fault category prediction. Experiments on the constructed HTS fault dataset and two public industrial inspection datasets demonstrate that RdR-Med consistently outperforms conventional direct VLM matching approaches and standard convolutional neural network baselines in terms of classification accuracy. By integrating cloud-based knowledge sharing with edge-side real-time perception, the proposed method significantly enhances the scalability, robustness, generalization, and interpretability of HTS fault detection.

title: CyberRoBERTa: A Lightweight Transformer-Based Language Model for IoT Intrusion Detection
authors: Dhai Alhafi; Fatmah Alanazi
keywords: IoT intrusion detection; large language models; on-device deployment; lightweight transformer; network traffic classification; class imbalance; CICIoT2023; ToN-IoT; Edge-IIoTset; Internet of Things security
topics: Network Security and Intrusion Detection; Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting; Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning
abstract: With the accelerated proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) and its widespread use in sensitive areas such as healthcare, homes, and factories, security has become an increasingly critical concern. IoT remains one of the most challenging domains to secure, lacking the manageable scale, well-maintained software, and homogeneous environments of easily secured systems. Large language models (LLMs) have recently been applied to improve IoT security; however, most applications treat LLMs as "off-the-shelf" tools, creating a domain mismatch because model representations, tokenizers, and data collators are designed for natural language rather than network traffic. In this work, we present CyberRoBERTa, built specifically to test whether departing from off-the-shelf LLM components, through a domain-specific Unigram tokenizer and an IoT-specialized data collator, yields a genuine advantage for IoT intrusion detection. We instantiate this framework as a compact, 10.2-million-parameter model designed for fully self-contained, on-device operation. Using CICIoT2023, TON_IoT, and Edge-IIoTset, the model achieves a binary classification F1-score of 96% and a multiclass F1-score of 89.54%. We further validate these results in three ways: a comparison against a classical machine learning baseline shows comparable accuracy; isolating the tokenizer's contribution from pretraining scale shows its benefit holds under matched pretraining conditions; and evaluating class-imbalance interventions shows improved detection on the most data-scarce class.

title: DDS-Mamba-YOLO: Improved adaptive state-space modeling for tomato fruit and leaf disease detection
authors: Jiajun Zhu; Tim Bary; Louis Petit; Shangpeng Sun
keywords: plant leaf disease detection; Mamba; YOLO; selective state space models; occluded object detection; small object detection; edge deployment; greenhouse crop monitoring; autonomous agricultural robots
topics: Smart Agriculture and AI; Advanced Neural Network Applications; Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection
abstract: Tomato is one of the most extensively cultivated and economically important crops worldwide, particularly in large-scale greenhouse environments, where plant health monitoring and fruit detection are essential for smart crop management. Greenhouse environments present multiple challenges: dense structures can obscure early disease symptoms and fruits, and fruits across different maturity stages and sizes need to be detected accurately. Moreover, deploying detection models on edge devices carried by mobile robotic platforms faces strict constraints on model size and computational cost. In this study, we propose a novel hybrid detection framework, DDS-Mamba-You Only Look Once (YOLO), built upon Deformable Dynamic State-space (DDS) and Mamba, a selective state space model-based YOLO to tackle the aforementioned challenges while balancing detection performance and model size. Specifically, three modules are proposed to integrate into the Mamba-YOLO backbone to enhance the performance: (1) a Spatial Deformable Channel Module (SDCM), built upon spatial adaptive downsample modules to better capture occluded and small targets; (2) a Dysample upsampling module to preserve fine-grained features adaptively, and (3) a Long Short Fusion Refiner (LSFR) module, which combines a dual-branch split Mamba block with a convolutional feature refinement module to strengthen gradient propagation and information flow. Experimental results on an image dataset collected from real greenhouse environments show that our model, with only 3.28M parameters and 8.3 GFLOPs, achieves 93.3% mAP@50-95 and 98.1% mAP@50, surpassing seven comparably-sized YOLO series models and three recent leaf disease detection models. Ablation experiments further validate the necessity of each module and its complementary interactions. Beyond training the model, we further establish a preliminary prototype that couples the DDS-Mamba-YOLO model with quadruped robot-based autonomous greenhouse inspection and Large Language Model (LLM)-based management consultation. This integrated system validates the practical deployment potential of the proposed model on edge devices and provides a preliminary blueprint for intelligent agricultural management at scale.

title: Deep Learning and N8N-Based Soybean Defect Recognition and Traceable Quality Grading System
source: International Journal of Research in Vocational Studies (IJRVOCAS)
authors: Rafie Hamizan Al Hafiz; Pola Risma; Hsien‐Wei Tseng; Chun-Chieh Fan
keywords: YOLOv11n; n8n workflow automation; quality grading; traceability; Gemini 2.5 Flash; edge deployment; Raspberry Pi; agricultural quality control; data augmentation
topics: Smart Agriculture and AI; Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection; Advanced Neural Network Applications
abstract: Soybean is an important food commodity whose market value is strongly influenced by seed quality. However, quality inspection in many small and medium agro-industries is still performed manually, making the process slow, subjective, and poorly documented. This study develops an automated soybean inspection system that combines deep-learning-based defect recognition with traceability-supported quality reporting through workflow automation. A YOLOv11n model was trained on a self-collected dataset of 344 annotated images covering five classes, namely Intact, Broken, Skin Damaged, Spotted, and Immature, which was expanded to 1,032 images through augmentation. The model runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 inspection station, where accumulated detection results are converted into a defect rate that determines the quality grade of each batch. An n8n workflow then forwards every inspection result to the Gemini 2.5 Flash large language model to generate a narrative quality-control report, and each batch is stored in an SQLite database that can be accessed through a history viewer to support traceability. Validation results show a precision of 92.73%, a recall of 90.71%, an mAP@0.50 of 96.54%, and an mAP@0.50–0.95 of 88.67%. Functional testing demonstrates that the system produces consistent grades, accumulates detections from multiple captures into a single batch, and generates reports automatically, while still producing a rule-based report when the language model service is unavailable. The proposed system therefore offers an automated, low-cost, and traceability-supported approach to soybean quality inspection that is suitable for deployment on edge devices.

title: Deepsite: A Next-Generation Vibe Coding Platform for Browser-Based Application Generation
source: International Research Journal on Advanced Engineering and Management (IRJAEM)
authors: Mahalingam M; Hariharan M; Elangkumaran B S; Chandru S; Hariragavan S V
keywords: large language models; AI-assisted software development; natural language programming; sand pack; Hugging Face Spaces; decentralized storage; software prototyping
topics: Software Engineering Research; Mobile and Web Applications; Software Engineering Techniques and Practices
abstract: DeepSite (v4) is a cloud-native, browser-based development platform designed to enable intuitive software creation through natural language interaction. With the growing capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), software development is evolving from manual coding toward intent-driven design. DeepSite addresses the challenges of this transition by providing a structured environment for generating, modifying, and executing AI-produced code efficiently. The platform integrates the Next.js App Router with Hugging Face serverless inference APIs to stream incremental code updates in real time. Instead of regenerating entire files, a constrained Search/Replace mechanism is employed to apply precise modifications, reducing token usage and minimizing inconsistencies. For execution, the system utilizes browser-based Web Containers (Sandpack), allowing instant preview without local setup. Project persistence is achieved through Hugging Face Spaces, enabling Git-based version control and decentralized storage without relying on traditional databases. The platform ensures scalability, security, and rapid prototyping by combining client-side execution with lightweight backend orchestration. This work demonstrates a practical approach to AI-assisted development and highlights the potential of browser-based environments in accelerating modern software engineering workflows.

title: Deploying LLM Transformer on Edge Computing Devices: A Survey of Strategies, Challenges, and Future Directions
authors: Endah Kristiani; Vinod Kumar Verma; Yang Chao-Tung
keywords: large language models; transformer models; edge computing; LLM deployment; model compression; inference optimization; resource-constrained devices; edge inference; privacy and security
topics: IoT and Edge/Fog Computing; Advanced Neural Network Applications; Topic Modeling
abstract: The intersection of edge computing, Large Language Models (LLMs), and the Transformer architecture is a very active and fascinating area of research. The core tension is that LLMs, which are built on the Transformer architecture, are massive and computationally intensive, while edge devices are resource-constrained in terms of power, memory, and processing capabilities. Therefore, LLMs based on the Transformer architecture are inherently unsuitable for edge computing in their original, full-sized form. They were designed for powerful, resource-rich cloud data centers. However, there is a massive and growing effort to make them suitable for edge devices. Implementing Transformer-based LLMs on edge computing devices is a complex but crucial task that requires a multi-faceted strategy. This paper reviews LLM deployment strategies for Transformer models on edge computing devices, examines the challenges, and estimates future directions. To address these challenges, researchers are exploring methods to compress LLMs and optimize their inference capabilities, making them more efficient for edge environments. Recent advancements in compact LLMs have shown promise in enhancing their deployment on edge devices, enabling improved performance while addressing the limitations of traditional models. This approach not only reduces computational costs but also enhances user privacy and security.
